newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: FOCUS-Swiss drugs giant Novartis wins final okay.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Swiss drugs giant Novartis wins final okay.

text.p: Swiss drugs majors Ciba-Geigy AG and Sandoz AG won long-awaited U.S. regulatory approval on Tuesday for their planned merger in what will become the world's number two pharmaceuticals giant.

Shares in both companies finished easier on profit-taking after the Federal Trade Commission said it had conditionally approved the merger, clearing away the last big obstacle to the mega-deal to create the new giant Novartis NOVZn.S, first announced in March.

"After only nine months of intensive preparations, we can now move forward with the task of building the world's leading life sciences company," Novartis chairman Alex Krauer, the former Ciba-Giegy boss, said in a statement.

The accord creates the world's biggest pharmaceutical company after Britain's Glaxo-Wellcome, with 4.4 percent of the world's fractured pharmaceuticals market. Glaxo-Welcome had 4.7 percent of the market in 1995.
Novartis had sales of 36 billion Swiss francs ($27 billion) in 1995 and spent 3.5 billion on research and development.

Novartis, the result of global consolidation among pharmaceutical companies, will focus on health care, agribusiness and nutrition. It will be a leading provider of generic drugs and have a broad range of health-care products.
Combined capitalisation would be more than 100 billion Swiss francs, overshadowing last year's merger of Glaxo and Wellcome.

"I think this shows the positive attitude about Novartis on the stock market," chief financial officer Raymund Breu told a news conference in Basle, noting that capitalisation had jumped by a third since the deal was first announced.

Breu said the partners would post a combined profit of around four billion francs in 1996, while merger costs this year would total two billion after after-tax charges of 3.5 billion are offset by divestment profits of 1.5 billion.

"You can calculate that the profits of Novartis will be around four billion Swiss francs in 1996 and so far this burden of two billion Swiss francs is something which doesn't weigh too heavily," Breu said.
Company officials would not make a detailed profit forecast for 1997, but new chief executive Daniel Vasella said he expected profit growth to continue next year.
The FTC said in Washington that Ciba and Sandoz must license or divest several product areas -- gene therapy, corn herbicides and flea-control markets -- to foster competition.
It said Sandoz had agreed to license some gene therapy technology and patent rights to France's Rhone-Poulenc Rorer so that it can compete against the new combined firm.
Sandoz had already agreed to sell its United States and Canadian corn herbicide business to Germany's BASF for about $780 million in one of the largest divestitures the FTC ever ordered.
Sandoz is also selling its flea control business to Central Garden & Pet Co in California or another FTC-approved buyer.
Ciba and Sandoz said in a joint statement the moves would not hurt them substantially, and analysts agreed.

"These are not massive cuts. Novartis will not lose any research potential in the long term," Union Bank of Switzerland analyst Birgit Kulhoff said, adding licensing deals in genetic therapy would preserve its access to key technology.
"It would have been bad if Novartis had to sell or reduce its stakes," she said.
The companies estimate the merger will save them about two billion Swiss francs over three years. They plan to cut the combined workforce by about 10 percent, or 13,000 jobs.
The merger of Sandoz and Ciba was approved by each company's shareholders in April and by the European Commission in July.
Both Sandoz and Ciba said in late October they expected the FTC to rule in late autumn on Novartis and officials close to the deal had said they expected a U.S. ruling by December 20.
Novartis shares will start trading on the Swiss Exchange on December 23.
Ciba shares closed one Swiss franc below an opening 1,626 om Tuesday and Sandoz was down one from 1,526 at the start of trading.
-- Zurich newsroom +41 1 631 7340 ($1=1.3228 Swiss Franc)
